title: Geometric heat pumping on a quantum processor
authors: Gerónimo J. Caselli, Luis O. Manuel, Liliana Arrachea, Pablo S. Cornaglia
abstract: Geometric heat pumping is the transfer of energy between reservoirs at equal temperature where the heat exchanged in an adiabatic cycle depends only on the driving contour in parameter space. We implement this mechanism on a superconducting quantum processor using a collision model, where a driven qubit interacts repeatedly with two ancilla qubits that are prepared in thermal states and emulate the reservoirs. Energy measurements before and after each interaction provide a calorimetric record of the heat exchanged with each reservoir. By reversing the driving contour, we extract a heat contribution associated with pumping. Its dependence on the period and on the contour follows exact simulations of the collision model, without adjustable parameters, and approaches in the slow-driving regime the geometric limit of the corresponding Lindblad dynamics.
summary: This paper demonstrates geometric heat pumping on a superconducting quantum processor by cyclically driving a qubit coupled to two thermal reservoirs. The authors show that the measurable, non-zero heat pumped is a geometric quantity determined by the path taken in parameter space. This bridges fundamental concepts from quantum thermodynamics and geometric phases to near-term quantum hardware implementations.
main_problem: The paper investigates geometric heat pumping—the transfer of energy between reservoirs at equal temperature—by cyclically driving a quantum system.
main_result: The pumped heat is shown to be a purely geometric quantity, depending only on the area enclosed by the driving contour in parameter space, and this is confirmed by comparing collision models to the adiabatic limit.
method: The authors employ a collision model implemented on a quantum processor, analyzing the system dynamics using both discrete time-stepping (collision model) and continuous-time adiabatic expansions.
model_or_system: The system is a working qubit coupled to two thermal reservoirs (L and R), modeled via a collision process involving ancilla qubits. The dynamics are described by a time-dependent Lindblad master equation.
key_observables: Stochastic heat exchanged per collision ($Q_{\alpha,j,k}$), ensemble average heat ($Q_c^\alpha$), and the geometric heat contribution ($Q_{geo}^\alpha$).
important_parameters: The slow-driving regime, the area enclosed by the driving contour, and the ratio of pumped heat to noise-induced heating.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the adiabatic approximation in the slow-driving limit to extract the geometric contribution, and the collision model assumes ancillas are reset after each interaction.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the quantum circuit for a single time cell, detailing the sequence of collisions and the structure of energy measurements ($E_{in}$ and $E_{out}$) used to calculate heat.
paper_structure: The paper moves from defining the physical setup and the collision model to deriving the continuous-time Lindblad dynamics. It then analyzes the slow-driving limit using adiabatic expansions to isolate the geometric heat term, benchmarking these results against direct simulations of the collision model.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, experimentally relevant platform (superconducting qubits) to test fundamental non-equilibrium thermodynamic principles, specifically linking quantum work extraction to geometric phases.
